nodes.title: Hold the nine fixed cells in one signal
nodes.why: The cells never move, so the template's @for tracks them by $index and play(i) addresses them by position. Keeping the array in a signal lets winner, isDraw and status recompute after every move.
nodes.alternative: Keep a plain board array and update a separate winner field in play() and reset().
nodes.tradeoff: Each move allocates a new nine-cell array, which costs nothing at this size, and no derived value can fall out of step with the board.

nodes.title: Compute the winner from the board
nodes.why: The winner is a function of the cells, so deriving it keeps it correct for the current board, and reset() only has to clear the board and the turn.
nodes.alternative: Set a winner field inside play() after each move and clear it in reset().
nodes.tradeoff: calculateWinner runs again on the first read after each board change, a negligible cost for eight lines, and there is no stored winner that reset() or a later undo feature could forget to clear.

nodes.title: Stop moves after game completion
nodes.why: play() rejects further moves after a win or draw, even when it is called from code instead of from an enabled cell.
nodes.alternative: Depend only on disabled cell buttons in the template.
nodes.tradeoff: The guard duplicates UI protection, but it preserves the game invariant for every caller.

nodes.title: Create the next board state

anchor.snippet: this.board.update((board) => board.map((cell, index) => (index === i ? mark : cell)));

nodes.why: board.update stores a new array with the mark at index i, so the signal registers a new value and winner, isDraw and status recompute before the turn check reads them.
nodes.alternative: Write the mark into board() in place, which leaves the signal holding the same array and every computed value stale.
nodes.tradeoff: Copying nine cells per move is negligible, and every move produces a separate board value.

nodes.title: Compare every winning triplet

anchor.snippet: if (v && v === b[c] && v === b[d]) return v;

nodes.why: A non-null mark that matches both remaining positions identifies the winner for that line.
nodes.alternative: Hard-code a winner check in play() for each possible move.
nodes.tradeoff: Iterating a line table is compact and testable, while custom board sizes would need generated combinations.
